paragraphs: What followed was almost an orgy, a feast open to everyone. Grushenka was the first to call for wine.
“I want to drink. I want to get properly drunk, like we did before. Do you remember, Mitya, do you remember how we became friends here last time!”
Mitya himself was almost delirious, sure that his happiness was close. But Grushenka kept sending him away from her.

“Go and have fun. Tell them to dance and make merry, ‘let the stove and cottage dance,’ like last time,” she kept calling out. She was tremendously excited. And Mitya hurried to obey her. The chorus was in the next room. The room where they had been sitting until then was too small, and cotton curtains divided it in two; behind them stood a huge bed with a puffy feather mattress and a pyramid of cotton pillows. In each of the four guest rooms there were beds. Grushenka settled herself right by the door. Mitya set an easy chair for her. She had sat in the same place to watch the dancing and singing “the time before,” when they had made merry there. All the girls who had come this time had been there then; the Jewish band with fiddles and zithers had come too, and at last the long-awaited cart had arrived with the wines and provisions.

Mitya bustled about. All sorts of people began coming into the room to look on, peasants and their women, who had been woken from sleep and drawn by the hope of another marvelous entertainment like the one they had enjoyed a month before. Mitya remembered their faces, greeting and embracing everyone he knew. He uncorked bottles and poured wine for anyone who showed up. Only the girls were keen on the champagne. The men preferred rum, brandy and, above all, hot punch. Mitya had chocolate made for all the girls, and ordered three samovars kept boiling all night, so that everyone could help themselves to tea and punch.

An absurd, chaotic confusion followed, but Mitya was in his natural element, and the more foolish it got, the higher his spirits rose. If the peasants had asked him for money just then, he would have pulled out his notes and handed them out left and right. That was probably why the landlord, Trifon Borissovitch, kept hovering around Mitya to protect him. He seemed to have given up any idea of going to bed that night; but he drank little, only one glass of punch, and kept a sharp lookout for Mitya’s interests in his own way. He stepped in at the right moment, politely and obsequiously persuading Mitya not to give away “cigars and Rhine wine,” and above all money, to the peasants as he had done before. He was also very indignant at the peasant girls drinking liqueur and eating sweets.
“They’re a lousy lot, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” he said. “I’d give every one of them a kick, and they’d take it as an honor—that’s all they’re worth!”

Mitya thought of Andrey again and ordered punch sent out to him. “I was rude to him just now,” he repeated in a sinking, softened voice. Kalganov did not want to drink, and at first did not care for the girls’ singing; but after a couple of glasses of champagne he became extraordinarily lively, strolling about the room, laughing, praising the music and the songs, admiring everyone and everything. Maximov, blissfully drunk, never left his side. Grushenka, too, was beginning to get drunk. Pointing to Kalganov, she said to Mitya:
“What a dear, charming boy he is!”

And Mitya, delighted, ran to kiss Kalganov and Maximov. Oh, his hopes were great! She had said nothing yet, and seemed, in fact, to hold back on purpose. But from time to time she looked at him with caressing, passionate eyes. At last she suddenly gripped his hand and pulled him hard toward her. She was sitting at that moment in the low chair by the door.
“How was it you came just now, eh? You just walked in!... I was frightened. So you wanted to give me up to him, did you? Did you really want to?”
“I didn’t want to spoil your happiness!” Mitya faltered blissfully. But she did not need his answer.
“Well, go and enjoy yourself ...” she sent him away once more. “Don’t cry, I’ll call you back.”

He would run off, and she listened to the singing and watched the dancing, though her eyes followed him wherever he went. But in another quarter of an hour she would call him again, and again he would run back to her.
“Come, sit beside me and tell me, how did you hear about me, and about my coming here yesterday? Who did you first hear it from?”
And Mitya began telling her all about it, disconnectedly, incoherently, feverishly. He spoke strangely, often frowning and stopping abruptly.
“What are you frowning at?” she asked.
“Nothing.... I left a man ill back there. I’d give ten years of my life for him to get well, to know he was all right!”

“Well, never mind him, if he’s ill. So you meant to shoot yourself tomorrow! What a silly boy! What for? I like reckless fellows like you,” she lisped, with a rather halting tongue. “So you’d go any length for me, eh? Did you really mean to shoot yourself tomorrow, you stupid? No, wait a little. Tomorrow I may have something to say to you.... I won’t say it today, but tomorrow. You’d like it to be today? No, I don’t want to today. Come, go along now, go and amuse yourself.”
Once, though, she called him over, puzzled and uneasy.

“Why are you sad? I can see you’re sad.... Yes, I see it,” she added, looking intently into his eyes. “Though you keep kissing the peasants and shouting, I can see something. No, be merry. I’m merry; you be merry, too.... I love somebody here. Guess who it is. Ah, look, my boy has fallen asleep, poor dear, he’s drunk.”

She meant Kalganov. He was in fact drunk and had dropped off for a moment, sitting on the sofa. But he was not merely drowsy from drink; he had suddenly felt dejected, or, as he said, “bored.” He was deeply depressed by the girls’ songs, which, as the drinking went on, gradually grew coarse and more reckless. The dances were just as bad. Two girls dressed up as bears, and a lively girl called Stepanida, with a stick in her hand, played the keeper and began to “show them.”
“Look alive, Marya, or you’ll get the stick!”
The bears rolled on the ground at last in the most unseemly way, amid roars of laughter from the closely packed crowd of men and women.
“Well, let them! Let them!” said Grushenka solemnly, with a look of ecstasy on her face. “When they do get a day to enjoy themselves, why shouldn’t folks be happy?”
Kalganov looked as though he had been smeared with dirt.
“It’s swinish, all this peasant foolery,” he murmured, moving away; “it’s the game they play when it’s light all night in summer.”
He particularly disliked one “new” song to a jaunty dance tune. It told how a gentleman came to try his luck with the girls, to see whether they would love him:
The master came to try the girls: Would they love him, or would they not?
But the girls could not love the master:
He would beat me cruelly, And such love is not for me.
Then a gypsy comes along, and he tries too:
The gypsy came to try the girls: Would they love him, or would they not?
But they couldn’t love the gypsy either:
He’d be a thief, I fear, And cause me many a tear.
And many more men come to try their luck, a soldier among them:
The soldier came to try the girls: Would they love him, or would they not?
But the soldier is rejected with contempt, in two indecent lines, sung with total frankness and causing a furore in the audience. The song ends with a merchant:
The merchant came to try the girls: Would they love him, or would they not?
And it turns out that he wins their love, because:
The merchant will make gold for me, And his queen I’ll gladly be.
Kalganov was downright indignant.

“That’s just a song of yesterday,” he said aloud. “Who writes such stuff for them? They might just as well have had a railwayman or a Jew come to try his luck with the girls; he’d have swept the field.”

And, almost as if it were a personal insult, he declared on the spot that he was bored, sat down on the sofa and fell asleep at once. His pretty little face looked rather pale as it fell back against the sofa cushion.
“Look how pretty he is,” said Grushenka, taking Mitya up to him. “I was combing his hair just now; his hair’s like flax, and so thick....”
And, bending over him tenderly, she kissed his forehead. Kalganov opened his eyes at once, looked at her, stood up, and with a very anxious air asked where Maximov was.
“So that’s who you want.” Grushenka laughed. “Stay with me a minute. Mitya, run and find his Maximov.”

Maximov, it turned out, could not tear himself away from the girls, and only ran off from time to time to pour himself a glass of liqueur. He had drunk two cups of chocolate. His face was red and his nose crimson; his eyes were moist and sickly sweet. He ran up and announced that he was going to dance the “sabotière.”
“They taught me all those well-bred, aristocratic dances when I was little....”
“Go, go with him, Mitya, and I’ll watch from here how he dances,” said Grushenka.

“No, no, I’m coming to watch too,” exclaimed Kalganov, brushing aside in the most naïve way Grushenka’s offer to sit with him. They all went to watch. Maximov danced his dance. But it won no great admiration from anyone but Mitya. It consisted of nothing but skipping and hopping, kicking up the feet, and at every skip Maximov slapped the upturned sole of his foot. Kalganov did not like it at all, but Mitya kissed the dancer.
“Thanks. You’re tired, perhaps? What are you looking for here? Would you like some sweets? A cigar, maybe?”
“A cigarette.”
“Don’t you want a drink?”
“I’ll just have a liqueur.... Have you any chocolates?”
“Yes, there’s a heap of them on the table there. Choose one, my dear soul!”
“I like one with vanilla ... for old people. He he!”
“No, brother, we haven’t got that special sort.”
“I say,” the old man bent down to whisper in Mitya’s ear. “That girl there, little Marya, he he! How would it be if you helped me make friends with her?”
“So that’s what you’re after! No, brother, that won’t do!”
“I’d do no harm to anyone,” Maximov muttered disconsolately.
“Oh, all right, all right. They only come here to dance and sing, you know, brother. But damn it all, wait a bit!... Eat and drink and be merry, meanwhile. Don’t you want money?”
“Later on, perhaps,” smiled Maximov.
“All right, all right....”

Mitya’s head was burning. He went out onto the wooden balcony that ran around the whole building on the inner side, overlooking the courtyard. The fresh air revived him. He stood alone in a dark corner and suddenly clutched his head in both hands. His scattered thoughts came together; his sensations blended into a whole and threw a sudden light into his mind. A fearful and terrible light! “If I’m to shoot myself, why not now?” passed through his mind. “Why not go for the pistols, bring them here, and make an end of it here, in this dark, dirty corner?” For almost a minute he stood undecided. A few hours earlier, when he had been dashing here, disgrace had been pursuing him, and the theft he had committed, and that blood, that blood!... But still it was easier for him then. Then everything was over: he had lost her, given her up. She was gone, for him—oh, then his death sentence had been easier to bear; at least it had seemed necessary, inevitable, for what had he to stay on earth for?

But now? Was it the same as then? Now one phantom, one terror at least was at an end: that first, rightful lover, that fateful figure had vanished without a trace. The terrible phantom had turned into something so small, so comic; it had been carried into the bedroom and locked in. It would never return. She was ashamed, and from her eyes he could see now whom she loved. Now he had everything to make life happy ... but he could not go on living, he could not; oh, damnation! “O God! Bring back to life the man I knocked down at the fence! Let this fearful cup pass from me! Lord, You have worked miracles for sinners like me! But what, what if the old man’s alive? Oh, then I would wipe away the shame of the other disgrace. I would restore the stolen money. I’d give it back; I’d get it somehow.... No trace of that shame will remain except in my heart forever! But no, no; oh, impossible, cowardly dreams! Oh, damnation!”

Yet there was a ray of light and hope in his darkness. He jumped up and ran back to the room—to her, to her, his queen forever! Was not one moment of her love worth all the rest of life, even in the agonies of disgrace? This wild question clutched at his heart. “To her, to her alone, to see her, to hear her, to think of nothing, to forget everything, if only for that night, for an hour, for a moment!” Just as he turned from the balcony into the passage, he came upon the landlord, Trifon Borissovitch. He thought the man looked gloomy and worried, and imagined he had come to find him.
“What is it, Trifon Borissovitch? Are you looking for me?”
“No, sir.” The landlord seemed disconcerted. “Why should I be looking for you? Where have you been?”
“Why do you look so glum? You’re not angry, are you? Wait a bit, you’ll soon get to bed.... What’s the time?”
“It’ll be three o’clock. Past three, it must be.”
“We’ll leave off soon. We’ll leave off.”
“Don’t mention it; it doesn’t matter. Keep it up as long as you like....”

“What’s the matter with him?” Mitya wondered for an instant, and he ran back to the room where the girls were dancing. But she was not there. She was not in the blue room either; there was no one but Kalganov asleep on the sofa. Mitya peeped behind the curtain—she was there. She was sitting in the corner, on a trunk. Bent forward, with her head and arms on the bed beside her, she was crying bitterly, doing her utmost to stifle her sobs so as not to be heard. Seeing Mitya, she beckoned him over, and when he ran to her, she gripped his hand tightly.

“Mitya, Mitya, I loved him, you know. How I have loved him these five years, all that time! Did I love him, or only my own anger? No, him, him! It’s a lie that it was my anger I loved and not him. Mitya, I was only seventeen then; he was so kind to me, so merry; he used to sing to me.... Or so it seemed to a silly girl like me.... And now, O Lord, it’s not the same man. Even his face is not the same; he’s different altogether. I wouldn’t have known him. I drove here with Timofey, and all the way I kept thinking how I would meet him, what I would say to him, how we would look at one another. My soul was faint, and all of a sudden it was as if he had emptied a pail of dirty water over me. He talked to me like a schoolmaster, all so grave and learned; he met me so solemnly that I was struck dumb. I couldn’t get a word in. At first I thought he was ashamed to talk in front of his great big Pole. I sat staring at him, wondering why I couldn’t say a word to him now. It must have been his wife that ruined him; you know he threw me over to get married. She must have changed him like that. Mitya, how shameful it is! Oh, Mitya, I’m ashamed, I’m ashamed for the rest of my life. Curse it, curse it, curse those five years!”
